newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: S&P affirms Westpac, may up Bank Melbourne.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Westpac, may up Bank Melbourne.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said it has affirmed the AA-minus long term and A1 plus short term counterparty ratings for Westpac Banking Corp.
It has also placed the A-minus long term and A2 short term counterparty ratings for the Bank of Melbourne Ltd on CreditWatch positive.
S&P said the actions were based on the announced terms and conditions of the proposed merger between the two banks made earlier on Thursday.
Westpac is proposing to acquire Bank of Melbourne ordinary and preference shares in a one-for-one share swap plus cash, or all cash, for a total acquisition price of A$1.435 billion.

The affirmation of Westpac's ratings reflected S&P's view that while higher gearing and integration costs arising from the acquisition would adversely impact the near-term performance, the acquisition of Bank of Melbourne was strategically positive in the long term.
Such a merger was subject to necessary approvals from regulatory authorities and Bank of Melbourne's shareholders.

"If successfully implemented, the acquisition would enhance Westpac's market share of Australian banking Australian dollar assets to 17.7 percent from 15.5 percent, positioning Westpac as equal second-largest domestic bank alongside Commonwealth Bank of Australia," S&P said.
"This action accords with Westpac's strategic focus on Australasia, and complements Westpac's position as the largest bank in New Zealand following its purchase of Trust Bank of New Zealand."

More importantly S&P said the acquisition would assist Westpac to overcome its present weakness of being under-represented in the state of Victoria, where it had only a 9.0 percent share of loans at December 31, 1996.
The placement of Bank of Melbourne's ratings on Creditwatch positive reflected the possible status, should the acquisition proceed, of becoming a fully owned and integral part of the Westpac Group.

S&P would continue to monitor developments surrounding the proposed acquisition, particularly the Federal government's response following the expected release of the findings of the Wallis inquiry into the Australian financial sector.
